passage: Sumit, sit. You look like someone who's been shut out. Let me tell you what happened to me, Zubin, at your age. My closest friend, Behram, lost his place in the university hockey team, and something went out of him. When I knocked on his door, he said, "Just leave me alone, Zubin." I was hurt. Honestly, I was angry. I'd been a good friend! For two days I sulked. Then I wrote him a postcard: "No need to reply. I'm around whenever you want. Chai on me." I sent one every Sunday, nothing heavy. I also asked his mother quietly whether he was safe; she said he was eating and sleeping, just very low. In the fourth month, a postcard came back with one line: "Is the chai offer still open?" If I had kept banging on his door, I think it would have stayed shut.

qa.q: What did Zubin write on the first postcard?
qa.a: No need to reply. I'm around whenever you want. Chai on me.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when Behram said "leave me alone"?
qa.a: Zubin felt hurt and rejected, even angry, and sulked for two days.

qa.q: Which choice let Zubin respect Behram's pace safely?
qa.a: Zubin quietly asked Behram's mother whether he was safe, and on hearing he was, kept sending gentle weekly postcards instead of pushing.

qa.q: What might the Sunday postcards have meant to Behram in those months?
qa.a: They showed Behram that a friend was still there without demanding anything, so he could come back when he was ready.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling feeling rejected when a friend pushed Zubin away, and keeping the door open with low-pressure messages while checking he was safe.

passage: The monsoon had knocked out power in Damini's hostel for the third evening when her friend Afreen's message finally came: "Please stop checking on me. Just leave me alone." Damini read it by torchlight and felt her face burn. She had called every day since Afreen went home after leaving the course. She typed three angry replies and deleted them all. Instead she wrote, "Okay. I'll stop asking questions. I'm still here whenever you want." After that she sent only small things every few days: a photo of the canteen cat, a song, no questions. Two weeks later, at midnight, Afreen wrote, "Thanks for everything. It won't matter much soon." Damini's stomach dropped. This was different. She phoned Afreen's elder sister at once, then a helpline for advice, and stayed awake until the sister messaged: "I'm with Afreen now. We're going to the doctor."

qa.q: What did Damini send after that first message?
qa.a: Only small things every few days: a photo of the canteen cat, a song, no questions.

qa.q: How did Damini feel reading "leave me alone", and how can you tell?
qa.a: Hurt and rejected, even angry; her face burned and she typed three angry replies before deleting them.

qa.q: Why did Damini change her approach after the midnight message?
qa.a: "It won't matter much soon" sounded like danger, so waiting was no longer right; she phoned Afreen's sister and a helpline at once.

qa.q: How might Afreen have seen the no-questions messages?
qa.a: They may have felt safe and unpressured, keeping a door open with a friend while Afreen had no energy to talk.

grounding: It shows a friend who feels rejected when told to leave someone alone, stays gently reachable at their pace, and acts at once when a message sounds like danger.

passage: I'm Dolma, and I'll tell you honestly what it was like when Tanvir dropped out and told me, "Just leave me alone." I was hurt. I'd been his friend since school. For a day I was angry: fine, I'll leave you alone forever. Then I cooled down. I didn't flood him with messages. Every Sunday I sent one line: "No need to reply. Thinking of you. Chai at the usual place if you ever want." I knew that if he ever said anything about hurting himself, I'd go straight to his house and call his family. He never did, and for two months he never replied. Then one Sunday he wrote, "Chai?" I cried a bit in the auto. We just sat there. I'm glad I kept the door open.

qa.q: What did Dolma send every Sunday?
qa.a: "No need to reply. Thinking of you. Chai at the usual place if you ever want."

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when Tanvir said "Just leave me alone"?
qa.a: Dolma felt hurt and rejected, then angry for a day, before calming down.

qa.q: What made Dolma's approach wise?
qa.a: Dolma stayed gently reachable with one low-pressure message a week, respected Tanvir's pace and was ready to act if there was any danger.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have felt reading the weekly messages?
qa.a: He may have felt cared for without pressure, which helped him reach out when he was ready.

grounding: Shows a friend who feels rejected when told to leave someone alone, but stays gently reachable with low-pressure messages and respects his pace, alert to danger.

passage:
Monday: Damini knocked on Vaibhav's hostel door with a plate of poha. He opened it a crack. "I said I want to be left alone, Damini." The door shut. She stood in the corridor, face burning, feeling rejected.
Wednesday: She almost didn't bother. Then she texted: "No pressure to reply. I'm around this week if you want company, or just a walk. No questions." She didn't text again.
Saturday: Her phone buzzed at nine. "Sorry about Monday. Can we get chai? I'm not great." Damini replied, "Of course. Ten minutes." At the stall he talked about his results for an hour. She just listened. At the end he said, "Thanks for not giving up."

qa.q: What did Damini bring to Vaibhav's door?
qa.a: A plate of poha.

qa.q: How did Damini feel when Vaibhav shut the door?
qa.a: She felt rejected and embarrassed, her face burning in the corridor.

qa.q: What did Damini do that kept the door open?
qa.a: She sent one low-pressure message offering company without questions and then respected his pace.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt when he texted on Saturday?
qa.a: He likely felt sorry about Monday and ready to lean on someone, since he said he was not great.

grounding: Shows a friend who feels rejected when pushed away, then stays reachable with a low-pressure message and respects the other's pace.

passage: "Lalit, your friend won't answer your calls and told you to stop bothering him? Let me tell you about Harbans. When we were twenty-one, his father's shop burnt down, and he stopped speaking to everyone, even me. He said, 'Sumit, go away.' I was so hurt I didn't sleep that night. But I didn't go away, and I didn't push. Every month I posted him a postcard. Just one line. 'Still here. Cricket on Sunday if you like.' Once his mother told me he'd said something frightening, and I went to their house that same evening and sat with him till his uncle came. Otherwise I let him be. After eight months, he turned up at the ground with his old bat. So, beta, one message. Then patience."

qa.q: What did Sumit post to Harbans every month?
qa.a: A postcard with one line: 'Still here. Cricket on Sunday if you like.'

qa.q: How did young Sumit feel when Harbans told him to go away?
qa.a: Sumit felt so hurt and rejected that sleep wouldn't come that night.

qa.q: What choices inside the story kept the friendship alive?
qa.a: Sumit stayed reachable with low-pressure postcards, respected Harbans's pace and went straight over when there was a sign of danger.

qa.q: How might Harbans have felt turning up with his old bat?
qa.a: He may have felt ready again and grateful that his friend had waited for him.

grounding: An elder recalls a friend who pushed the elder away and how staying gently reachable, respecting pace and acting when there was danger kept the door open.

passage:
Maria had moved to Pune for work, and her best friend Anjali was back in Kochi, having a terrible year. In exam week, when Maria's own deadlines were piling up, she finally called.
"Just leave me alone, Maria," Anjali said, and hung up.
Maria stared at the phone. It felt like a slap. Part of her was angry. I've been trying for months. Fine.
But she remembered what Anjali's mother had told her: Anjali was safe at home and seeing a doctor, just very low.
So Maria didn't push, and she didn't disappear. Every few days she sent something small. "No need to reply. Saw a boat like the one we took in Alleppey. Thinking of you." Then, "Still here whenever."
Nine days later, a message came. "Sorry I was rude. Can we talk Sunday?" Maria smiled and wrote, "Always."

qa.q: How many days later did Anjali's message come?
qa.a: Nine days later.

qa.q: How did Maria feel when Anjali hung up?
qa.a: She felt rejected and angry, as if she'd been slapped after months of trying.

qa.q: What did Maria do that kept the door open?
qa.a: She respected Anjali's pace, knowing Anjali was safe, and stayed gently reachable with small no-pressure messages.

qa.q: How might Anjali see Maria's small messages?
qa.a: She probably felt cared for without being pushed, and came to admire her friend's patience, which made it easier to reply.

grounding: Maria feels rejected when her friend says leave me alone, but stays gently reachable with low-pressure messages and respects her pace, knowing she is safe.
